name: What this system does with the rules

text.content:
One page per screen: the printed rules it applies for you, and the ones it states and leaves to your call. Every line names the book and the page it comes from.

Every line in these pages names a book and a page. A figure you doubt is checked against the book on the table rather than against the software, and where the two differ the book wins: this system computes the rules, it does not arbitrate them.

The system works out what a rule is worth. It never decides when a rule applies. Nothing here runs a clock: a hazard interval, a maintenance period, a study week, a jump's hundred diameters are printed where you will be looking and are yours to apply. The combat round is the single exception, and only because a combat is advanced by hand. A wrong automatic number is worse than an absent one, because nobody checks it.

An attack roll never reads its target. What a dodge, a parry or an evasive manoeuvre costs the attacker is stated on the card for you to apply, and everything that needs a victim — armour, Lo-Pen, scale, radiation, a robot's hardening — is resolved when the damage is applied, where the target is known.

Some rules ship with a switch, and the switch starts off. Where two books print different procedures for the same thing, or where a book prints a rule as optional, both are built and a world setting decides which is in force: the Core's vehicle criticals or the 2026 Vehicle Handbook's, the Core's vacuum or the Companion's, the Companion's defence missiles and its layered missile defence, fleet battles, and a dozen more. The default is always the Core's, so a table that does not own the other book never gets its numbers by accident, and a page below that names a switched rule says so.

Where a rule is left to you, the screen says so where you are looking, not only here. These pages gather those statements in one place, so a table can see before play what it will be calling itself.

Page numbers are the ones printed on the page, so you can open the book straight at them.

22 screens: 212 rules applied for you, 18 left to your call.

What this screen handles for you

  • A check is 2D + the characteristic's DM + the skill's level, scored against one of eight difficulties, with Boon and Bane, and a faster or slower timeframe worth DM±2 (Core p.61-63).
  • The skill list says which kind of check is open: a named characteristic check at DM+0, or Not proficient at DM−3 where a skill is called for and the Traveller has none (Core p.58).
  • The attack modifiers are rows on the prompt rather than a number to remember — range band, cover, prone, the target's movement, and the Minor Actions spent aiming (Core p.74).
  • Beyond 100 m a shot is at Extreme range unless the weapon has a Scope. A table that plays the book's 300 m concession, or waives the rule, says so once in the world settings rather than on every roll (Core p.77).
  • A ground weapon fired at a spacecraft-scale target takes DM+2, and a spacecraft weapon fired at a ground target DM−2, declared with a tick beside cover and prone (Core p.167).
  • An Auto weapon picks its fire mode here — single, burst or full auto — and the aiming ladder greys out for the two modes that forfeit it (Core p.79).
  • A psionic power is rolled on the talent itself, with the PSI DM and the talent's level both in the formula, and a power pushed past its printed reach is priced in PSI before the roll (Core p.229).
  • A check can be chained off an earlier one, or set against another as an opposed check. Working together is the same control, and takes as many helpers as the table brings (Core p.62-63).
  • An attack resolves on the traits of the round that is loaded, not on the launcher's own, so a Smart or an AP round changes the shot it is fired in (Core p.77).
  • Inaccurate is two different rules under one name, and the prompt tells them apart by the trait itself: written with a score it is the flat DM past ten metres (Field Catalogue p.7); written bare it is the newer vehicle-weapon rule, which pushes the shot down the printed range bands instead (Core p.77).
  • Nothing that is a damage pool is offered as a characteristic to roll on — a vehicle's Hull, a robot's or a creature's Hits — and a creature attacks on its listed skill alone (Core p.84).

What it leaves to you

  • In zero gravity, the recoil check is yours to call. A close-combat weapon, or a ranged one without the Zero-G trait, owes an Average (8+) Athletics (dexterity) check or the attack misses outright and the shooter spins out of control. The prompt states the check and its target number beside the band, marks a Zero-G weapon exempt, and rolls nothing (Core p.81).

What this screen handles for you

  • The card scores the Effect against the difficulty that was set, or against the assumed Average (8+) where none was, and says which of the two it used rather than hiding the assumption (Core p.61).
  • The result band, and the card's own tone, are the six printed bands (Core p.61).
  • Every modifier that produced the roll is listed by name with its own DM, so a total can be argued with.
  • First aid off a Medic check — the Effect, minimum 1 point — is offered as a button on the card that earned it (Core p.82).
  • A psionic power's duration is rolled from the card, and the card states what the power cost the reserve, and what it cost the body when the reserve could not pay (Core p.229).

What this screen handles for you

  • Effect and the melee STR DM added to the damage roll (Core p.77)
  • a burst adding the Auto score, beside those two and outside the Reduced/Minimum transform (Core p.79)
  • Destructive multiplying the rolled total by 10, from the doubled D or the trait (Core p.78)
  • Protection subtracted, AP ignoring that much of it, Lo-Pen multiplying it (Core p.77, Field Catalogue p.7)
  • a spacecraft-scale target ignoring AP from a Ground weapon (Core p.79)
  • an Effect 6+ attack always inflicting at least 1 point (Core p.77)
  • Stun taken off END alone, the excess reported as rounds of incapacitation (Core p.79)
  • Ground/Spacecraft ×10 and ÷10 with rounding down, applied after Effect and Destructive and before the armour deduction (Core p.167)
  • the mount's own damage multiple applied after the armour deduction (High Guard p.29, Core p.168)
  • the five Companion damage-response traits, and the rule that an excepted damage type gets through in full (Companion p.93-94)
  • which facing was struck is picked on the card — the Core's five or the 2026 book's six, whichever procedure the world is running — and the armour that answers is that facing's (Core p.140)
  • where END's overflow goes is the target's own choice, given once as the order of their damage chain rather than asked at every blow (Core p.77)

What this screen handles for you

  • Damage runs down the chain the Traveller declares — END first, as printed — and the rest follows from it: unconscious when a link past the first empties, dead when the whole chain is empty, and every characteristic's DM recomputed from the value it has been reduced to (Core p.77).
  • Where END's overflow goes is the target's own choice, given once as the order of that chain and reorderable in play (Core p.77).
  • First aid is the Effect of a Medic check, minimum 1 point, shared out as the medic likes and once per injury. The two conditions no sheet can know — equipment to hand, within the minute — are put to the referee in the dialog (Core p.82).
  • What treatment is owed derives from the wounds rather than being ticked: surgery at three damaged characteristics, medical care at one or two (Core p.82).
  • Medical care restores 3 + END DM + the Medic's level, divided evenly; natural healing is 1D + END DM a day, or the END DM alone while surgery is still owed — which on a negative DM makes the patient worse (Core p.82).
  • Coming round is an END check a minute with a cumulative DM+1 per failure, and one fresh point of damage puts a Traveller who has just woken straight back down (Core p.82).
  • INT and EDU heal a point a day, and PSI is not in that set (Core p.83).
  • The highest augment TL is shown beside the two procedures it penalises, without the sheet guessing which implant is relevant (Core p.83).
  • Radiation is two readings of the same six thresholds — the dose taken now, and the running total that costs END permanently — with the armour's Rad rating deducted from every dose (Core p.81, p.100).
  • A disease or a poison opens its check on Endurance, as the book fixes it, keeping its own difficulty and interval; the interval is printed and never scheduled (Core p.80).
  • Fatigue is DM−2 to every check, ticked by hand, because the three things that cause it are hours no sheet can watch (Core p.80).
  • Encumbrance is DM−2 on physical actions and only those. The threshold is STR + END plus the skills that raise it, worn armour counting a quarter of its mass and nothing at all while powered (Core p.98).
  • Armour a Traveller is not trained for costs DM−1 per level short, or a flat DM−3 with no such skill at all (Core p.100).
  • A psionic power spends its listed cost on a success and one point on a failure, the excess below zero arriving as damage; a Traveller with an empty reserve is refused the attempt (Core p.229).
  • Training is eight-week Study Periods, as many as the level being reached, each ending on an Average (8+) EDU check (Core p.55).

What this screen handles for you

  • One sheet for a person and for a creature, the preset deciding which. A person takes damage END first, like any Traveller (Core p.77).
  • A creature's four states run off Hits alone: driven off at half, unconscious at 0.9×, dead at its full score, destroyed at twice it (Core p.84-85).
  • A creature adds nothing to melee damage, having no STR, and Stun incapacitates it at half Hits rather than off END (Core p.84).
  • Fast and Slow Metabolism feed Initiative directly (Core p.85).
  • The Fight or Flight table is transcribed row for row, Hunter's conditional 6+ included, with the four patterns whose attack side is a scene fact left as one (Core p.90).
  • The animal size table is held as advice and never as arithmetic: the sheet says whether the numbers agree with it and never overrides them (Core p.89).

What this screen handles for you

  • Five armour facings, the roof at half the sides and the floor at half the rear (Core p.140).
  • The bonus to hit a vehicle is read off its shipping size, row for row (Core p.140).
  • Against a weapon under 4D, or one with Stun, a vehicle gains extra armour equal to its TL on every facing — applied when the damage lands, not printed and forgotten (Core p.140).
  • Criticals: severity is Effect − 5, a repeat takes the higher of the new one and the old plus one, the cap is 6, and 6D of overflow ignores armour. The sustained-damage ladder fires every tenth of starting Hull (Core p.140-141).
  • Agility penalties for running outside the chassis's native medium, and for towing, are read off the vehicle rather than typed (Vehicle Handbook Update 2026 p.16, p.35).
  • Two editions of the vehicle combat rules ship and a world setting says which is in force: the Core's by default, or the 2026 Vehicle Handbook's Structure, critical table, destruction thresholds, collision procedure, six facings and called shot as one block, because they are one machine and no book prints them mixed (Vehicle Handbook p.10).
  • An Ion hit on a vehicle is a disruption and not a wound: it takes no Hull, and clearing it is done by hand (Central Supply Catalogue p.151).
  • Dogfighting and evasive action are opposed checks made by whoever is at the controls, on their own skill, with the vehicle's Agility as a modifier they can waive. What the result costs an attacker shooting at the vehicle is stated on the card for the referee to apply (Core p.138).

What this screen handles for you

  • The construction side is the printed one end to end: hull points by size band, configuration and hull options, armour by material with its TL cap and the Military Hull doubling, drive potentials, bridges, sensors, a power budget whose consumers can be switched off, crew requirements with the capital-ship reduction, fuel by the four-week period, mortgage and maintenance (Core p.171).
  • Ship criticals are transcribed whole, including the sixteen cells that raise the Hull severity instead of damaging their own location (Core p.169-170).
  • Initiative is the pilot's skill plus effective thrust, so an M-Drive critical moves it on its own (Core p.165).
  • A gunner fires from the crew roster, on their own skill and characteristic, with the mount's fire control and — on a sensors check — the suite's grade (Core p.167).
  • Two or more weapons of the same kind in one turret fire as one attack at +1 per damage die, and the mount's own damage multiple — ×3 for a barbette up to ×1000 for a spinal — is applied after the target's armour (Core p.168, High Guard p.29).
  • A station action opens the same prompt as any other check, seeded from the crew member sitting at it, and the ship's own DMs ride it as modifiers a referee can untick rather than as numbers welded into the formula (Core p.167).
  • A hull may carry two computers — a primary and a backup on a lower Processing score, never both at once — and every derivation reads whichever one is live, so a fallback changes what the ship can run (High Guard p.20).
  • /bis is a pool ring-fenced for Jump Control and worth +5 to that program alone, and /fib makes a computer immune to Ion weapons; both are fitted per computer, which is what makes a hardened primary over an unhardened backup a case the books are about (High Guard p.20).
  • An Ion hit deducts Power and computer Bandwidth without moving a Hull point, and a computer rated /fib takes neither (High Guard p.30).
  • A hull may carry a reaction drive beside its manoeuvre drive: while it burns, the two Thrusts add and it spends fuel where the other draws Power, and the G-force the compensators cannot cover is read out with the rung it costs the crew (High Guard p.16, p.17).
  • Any parts-list row that draws Power can be Hardened at +50 % of its cost, which is what gives the fleet Trait's 75 % of systems that use Power a denominator to count against (High Guard p.61, p.111).
  • Maintenance is a stamp and not a counter: the ship records when it was last serviced and the sheet says how many four-week periods it is behind, worked out when the sheet is drawn (Core p.153, p.154).
  • The bay tables, the mount capacities and the size limits on a hull option are read as advice: a printed statblock is transcribed as printed and the design checks say where it disagrees with the book, rather than overwriting the figure (High Guard p.12, p.57, p.61).
  • The Install Hull Options list is priced per ton of hull with its printed exclusions — Reflec against Stealth, solar coating against nearly everything, Stealth's own tonnage and sensor DM below TL10 (High Guard p.13, p.14).

What it leaves to you

  • When a ship's Power and Bandwidth come back after an Ion hit is yours to say. Both losses sit on the sheet as figures with an eraser beside them, because the book deducts them temporarily and never says when the temporary ends — so nothing here schedules a recovery (High Guard p.30).
  • Maintenance is displayed and never enforced. The ship carries the day it was last serviced and the header says how many four-week periods it is behind; nothing bills it, nothing degrades the ship for it, and the once-a-year shipyard visit is stated as a sentence rather than derived, this system having no year length to measure it against (Core p.153, p.154).

What this screen handles for you

  • The size table drives slots, Hits, the attack DM, spaces and cost; locomotion carries its own agility and endurance figures; armour is by TL band with the slots-per-point rule (Robot Handbook p.13).
  • A robot is wrecked at Hits 0 and destroyed at twice its starting Hits (Robot Handbook p.13).
  • The brain's grade sets the hardest task it may attempt — Difficult for an Advanced brain up to Impossible for a Conscious one. The prompt says so as a caption and never refuses the roll, because the same page lets outside modifiers bring a task back within reach; it applies to INT, EDU and SOC checks alone, and taking longer counts (Robot Handbook p.115).
  • A brain's skill DM reaches a check through the robot's own INT, so an upgraded brain is worth what the upgrade says (Robot Handbook p.66).
  • Ion weapons ignore armour, take no Hits and shut the brain down for as many rounds as the damage rolled; a hardened brain is immune (Robot Handbook p.106).
  • A stunner meets half a robot's Protection, and what gets through is an ordinary wound rather than stun damage (Robot Handbook p.106).
  • A locomotion of None is a robot that cannot move rather than one that moves at zero: it has no Agility and no speed, and the sheet prints a dash where a number would be a lie (Robot Handbook p.16).
  • A robot running on RTG or solar power alone takes the printed degradation — half its speed, half its STR and Agility −2 — and a second such source fitted alongside cancels it, which is the clause the rule turns on (Robot Handbook p.55).
  • Radiation is counted against the brain: every 1000 rads costs INT−1 and Bandwidth−1, a hardened brain halves the dose, and INT 0 is inoperable. A Basic or Hunter/Killer brain takes DM−1 at INT 2 and DM−2 at INT 1 (Robot Handbook p.106).

What this screen handles for you

  • A weapon carries its range with a melee flag, its damage, its damage types as a set, its magazine and what is loaded in it, its scale, fire control, power and traits. Armour carries its protection, the skill and level it asks for, and whether it is powered.
  • Damage is typed as the book prints it — a score written with D, a doubled D, or a die of another size — and the sheet keeps the book's own spelling.
  • A magazine counts shots. An ordinary shot spends one round, a burst the Auto score, full auto three times it. A mode the magazine cannot pay for is refused, and an empty weapon is refused before the prompt opens (Core p.77, p.79).
  • Reloading is a whole magazine and one Minor Action — three of them on a Slow Loader (3) weapon — stated on the control and never spent, this system keeping no action budget (Core p.75, Field Catalogue p.7).
  • An Auto weapon prints what each fire mode costs it, beside the magazine that figure is read against (Core p.79).
  • A disease or a poison carries difficulty, damage, effect and interval, which is the four-slot shape the book prints (Core p.80).
  • A device rated Computer/0 is a real rating and not an absence: an augment, a suit of armour and a piece of equipment can each host software, and nothing fitted stays a third state the sheet can say (Core p.104, p.106, Central Supply Catalogue p.27).
  • A host may be specialised — rated for one kind of program only, which is what a wafer jack's Expert bonus is — so its score answers for that kind and for nothing else (Core p.112, Central Supply Catalogue p.61).
  • The trait registry ships names and parameter shapes and no rules text, which is what lets the prompt sort every trait into one that is applied, one that is offered, and one that is only a reminder.

What this screen handles for you

  • A person's Initiative is the Effect of the DEX or INT check and never the total, whether it is rolled from the sheet or from the tracker (Core p.73).
  • A ship rolls 2D + the pilot's Pilot skill + Thrust, and in a space combat the whole crew reads back the one roll the ship made (Core p.165).
  • A tie is broken on the higher DEX before anyone acts simultaneously (Core p.73).
  • Ambush and the commander's Tactics Effect ride the initiative roll, and a combatant who is surprised is refused the Tactics check the rule opens with (Core p.73).

What this screen handles for you

  • A creation check is 2D plus the DM the printed table names, and nothing else (Core p.11). This is the one place the system refuses its own roll prompt: the modifiers of play have no business in a qualification roll.
  • Both creation limits, and they are not the same shape (Core p.18, Core p.55). Level 4 is a ceiling and the excess is discarded silently, as printed; the 3 × (INT + EDU) cap degrades instead, landing the skill at level 0, which is the only procedure the books print for passing it — refusing the grant outright would leave the table with a printed skill and nowhere to put it.
  • Background skills are EDU DM + 3, clamped to 0-6 by the book's own parenthesis (Core p.18).
  • The Connections Rule (Core p.19): at most two, each with a different Traveller, never above level 3 and never Jack-of-All-Trades. A connection and a contact are two outcomes of one agreement and both sides are written, which is the transaction a single sheet cannot express.
  • Ageing: the DM is the career's own ageing law read against the eight printed rows (Core p.49), the player chooses which characteristics take the loss (Core p.48), and an ageing crisis fails every later qualification roll automatically.
  • Advancement reads the highest rank reached (Core p.46), not the rank held now.
  • Mustering out (Core p.46-48): the Cash column at most three times across all careers, and the Benefit rolls kept as a running tally rather than counted back off the careers served, because some thirty printed rows wipe, grant, remove or retain rolls, and two let a player wager any number of them mid-term.
  • The shared skills package is drained in turn, one entry per Traveller (Core p.50), with a trailing number read as the level and its absence read as the book's own default.
  • Psionics needs no machinery of its own (Core p.228): the PSI test is 2D − the terms served, the two openings the Core prints differ only in who may take them, and the Psion career runs through the same term loop as any other.
  • A term counts when it closes and not when it is entered, which the books say three times: four years are credited even to a term cut short, Benefits are one roll per full term served, and ageing begins at the end of the fourth (Core p.11, p.46, p.48).
  • Qualification carries the conditional DMs a career actually prints — a DM per previous career, a DM if the last term was in a named career, a DM for a characteristic at a threshold — rather than one flat number (Bounty Hunter p.6).
  • A Benefit that is a voucher is redeemed against the referee's own library rather than invented, and the printed Other Benefits table is rolled instead of typed in (Core p.46, p.47).
  • Age is a sum of what each term actually cost and never 18 + 4 × terms — a Companion pre-career starts at 22 + 2D3, and a printed term is not always four years. Two Travellers who served two terms each can finish at different ages.

What it leaves to you

  • No career ships with the system. The printed careers are the publisher's own text, so character creation runs off career records a referee types in — there is a form for it — or off a module that carries them (Core p.11).

What this screen handles for you

  • The printed profile parses in eHex, 0-9 then A onwards skipping I and O (Core p.248), with X read as a starport that does not exist rather than as a digit. A sector-table line may carry its travel zone as a suffix — A788899-C A — because that is how a referee copies one.
  • The eighteen trade codes are tested off the profile rather than typed (Core p.261), and the travel zone joins them on the trade columns, because Amber and Red price Advanced Weapons without being facts about the world's economy (Core p.244).
  • All three cells whose digit means nothing alone are glossed — atmosphere, population and government, 45 entries (Core p.250, p.252, p.253).
  • Fuel follows the starport letter: A and B refine, C and D do not, E and X sell none (Core p.257).
  • The berthing rate is rolled once per starport and recorded, prices being stable at any given port (Core p.258). Null is a third state — not yet rolled — distinct from E, a port that charges nothing, and X, no port at all.
  • The per-planet, per-month trade state lives here and outlives any one screen: the search stamp that makes each further attempt this month DM−1 (Core p.241) and the refusal that locks a supplier out for a month (Core p.243).
  • A world is placed by the sector and hex the books print, its subsector worked out from them, so the distance between any two placed worlds is answered on demand. A sector the books do not name is a homebrew map and not an error (Core p.248).

What it leaves to you

  • What a Law Level bans is yours to read off the page. The book gives it as prose about categories of goods with no numbers under it, and this system does not print a paraphrase of a rulebook. The sheet gives you the Law Level; the one place the fact is numeric — a lot the Imperium bans outright — is a field on the lot itself (Core p.255).
  • There is no list of a world's jump neighbours. The distance between two placed worlds is worked out when you ask for it, and a voyage leg takes its parsecs typed, because either end of a leg may be a bare name on a napkin.

What this screen handles for you

  • The two printed checks are a task chain, in the order the book runs them: Easy (4+) Astrogation (EDU) to plot, then Easy (4+) Engineer (j-drive) modified by that chain (Core p.157).
  • Plotting takes DM−1 per parsec, entered as a waivable source that reads DM−1 per parsec ×3 rather than as an anonymous station DM (Core p.157).
  • Unrefined fuel is DM−2 on the jump check, read off the tank rather than typed (Core p.157).
  • Fuel is a flat 10 % of the hull per parsec whatever the drive is rated, and a jump of less than one parsec counts as jump-1 for both the fuel and the DM (Core p.157).
  • Both misjump procedures ship and a world setting says which is in force: the Core reads the failed Engineer check's Effect against three outcomes (Core p.158), the Companion reads the sum of both Effects for the trigger and each Effect on a variance table of its own (Companion p.150-153). The Core's "at the referee's option" third outcome, and its merciful substitute, are offered as options rather than promoted to results.
  • The day counter is the referee's, and this screen is the only thing that moves it: nothing schedules a jump and nothing ticks by itself.

What it leaves to you

  • Two of the three jump modifiers are printed beside the check and left to you — DM−4 for jumping inside the hundred-diameter limit, and DM−1 per month the ship is behind on maintenance. Nothing here tracks a position in a star system, and the months a ship is behind are counted on its own sheet without ever reaching this check, so the roll prompt takes both by hand (Core p.157).
  • After a bad jump, the two checks everyone aboard owes are printed and rolled by you. The crew are characters this screen does not own, and a roll made for a player by a window nobody is sitting at is the wrong side of the line this system draws (Companion p.151-152).

What this screen handles for you

  • Finding a supplier is a Traveller's own check and the book prints three of them: Average (8+) Broker for a supplier, Streetwise for a black-market one, and Admin for an online one on a TL8+ world, which takes hours where the other two take 1D days (Core p.241).
  • The search carries the starport's size and every search already made on this planet this month as a further DM−1 (Core p.241), counted off stamps on the world rather than off a number somebody remembers to reset.
  • The shelf is every Common good plus every good one of the world's codes matches, and rows 61-65 are a black market's alone (Core p.242).
  • The tonnage is banded onto the roll and not onto the result (Core p.242), and the whole shelf is rolled at once, so correcting a digit of the world profile re-reads the dice already rolled rather than rolling new ones.
  • One transaction is 3D + the trader's Broker − the other side's (Core p.243), with the hired local broker's own DM printed as a term of its own so a table can see whether it has already been typed into the box beside it (Core p.242).
  • A DM column takes the largest applicable and never the sum (Core p.243).
  • The smuggler's overlay: a locally banned good takes the world's Law Level minus the Level it is banned at, and the higher of the two Sale DMs wins (Core p.243).
  • The broker's fee is levied on the gross — 10 % for the local broker, 20 % for a fixer handling illegal goods (Core p.242) — so a brokered deal that only breaks even loses money twice, as printed.
  • Walking away stamps the refusal: no dealing with that supplier again for at least a month (Core p.243).
  • The screen stays everyone's (Core p.238): a player reads it, and the two writes — the search stamp and the refusal — take the referee.

What this screen handles for you

  • Two columns from both ends of the route, because population, Tech Level and the travel zone score differently for passengers and for freight (Core p.239, p.240). Traffic is a route and needs both worlds; a speculative market is one counter and needs one.
  • The Effect of one Average (8+) check leads both tables, and the printed skill lists differ: Broker, Carouse or Streetwise for passengers, Broker or Streetwise for freight (Core p.239, p.240).
  • The number of passengers available "cannot usually exceed the number of people resident" (Core p.239), and a Steward aboard adds the printed DM.
  • Freight comes in lots of 1D, 1D×5 and 1D×10 tons, and a lot cannot be broken up (Core p.240, p.241): a hold with room for part of one has no room for it.
  • Mail is offered on 12+ with the DM banded off the freight total, plus the armed-ship and low-TL terms, and it becomes an ordinary freight lot once taken — the book calls it "a special form of freight" (Core p.241).
  • Berths are consumed as printed: one stateroom per high passage, two basic passages sharing one, a low passenger taking a low berth, and an emergency low berth holding four (Core p.158, High Guard p.24).
  • A passage's baggage allowance is summed into the hold on the book's own conversion, so a full passenger deck costs cargo space rather than being free.
  • Lateness is measured at the moment of delivery (Core p.241) — the day is read when the consignment is settled, and no timer ever moves it.
  • Who pays when is the book's: a passage is collected when the berth is taken (Core p.239) and freight on delivery, which is why arrival moves money for one and not for the other.
  • Waking a low passenger is rolled from the arrival card: a Routine (6+) Medic check on INT taking 1D×10 minutes, with the ship's TL12 DM and its emergency-berth DM already on it and the END DM of whichever sleeper you target added by name (Core p.158).

What it leaves to you

  • A non-human passenger takes DM−2 on the revival check, and adding it is yours. The arrival card prints the modifier and the prompt leaves the row out, because a low berth holds a booking and a head count and never an Actor: nothing aboard says which sleepers are not human (Core p.158).

What this screen handles for you

  • The mortgage is the purchase price over the printed divisor, net of any Ship Shares contributed before it was calculated (Core p.149), with an override beside it because a hull bought outright, part-financed or taken as a career Benefit have three different legitimate mortgages.
  • How long it runs, and therefore what it costs in total, is read from the printed payment count (Core p.154) — the reading the purchase page owes and never states, and the one that shows the crew buying the hull roughly twice.
  • Every periodic figure runs on the four-week Maintenance Period (Core p.149, p.154, p.183; High Guard p.23).
  • Life support is billed three ways as printed: per stateroom, again per person not in a low berth, and a tenth of that per occupied low berth (Core p.154).
  • Fuel is a unit price and never a periodic charge (Core p.155), so it is priced where it is bought and never appears in the period's bill.
  • Skipping on Debts is one 2D against 8+ per new system entered, with all six printed terms drawn even when a term comes to zero (Core p.153) — two of them rates, one a referee's judgement over a printed span, one a four-way band, and one the local Law Level offset by a constant. It is not a task check and does not pretend to be one: no characteristic, no skill, no Effect.
  • The two facts the book says persist — the distance run since the crew were last discovered, and the overdue band — are the only two the screen records.
  • The transfer screen is the one place in the system that writes money on demand, and it does so on one explicit validation with the chat card as the record: direction, sum, every share, and every shortfall that became debt.

What it leaves to you

  • Skipped maintenance stays on paper. Nothing here counts the periods a ship has missed, so neither the Poor Maintenance roll — 2D against 8+ with a DM per period skipped, a critical hit on a success — nor the DM−1 per month on the jump check ever fires by itself. Both screens print the rule where you will be looking (Core p.154, p.157).
  • A ship holds no purse. The Travellers' credits are the only money the system moves; a hull's earnings reach the crew through the transfer screen, which writes the split and posts the record.

What this screen handles for you

  • A round resolves in the three named steps, and every ship takes a step before any ship takes the next (Core p.164).
  • The seven range bands are the state and the kilometres derive from them, never the other way round (Core p.165); the table is also read backwards for a referee who would rather type a distance.
  • On a scene built for space, dragging a token reads out the band the path crosses and the kilometres it is, and a path with no single reading says which reading failed rather than guessing (Core p.165).
  • Initiative is 2D + the pilot's Pilot skill + the ship's Thrust, rolled once for each ship and read back by every crew member, plus the commander's Tactics (naval) Effect scoped to that ship because the book scopes it there (Core p.165).
  • Thrust splits between movement and combat manoeuvring, only movement pays for a band change, and Thrust may be accumulated across rounds to pay for a change one round cannot afford (Core p.165, p.166). Two ships closing add what each puts into movement.
  • Evasive action is paid for with Thrust the pilot did not spend (Core p.171).
  • Pilot and captain are closed to one holder each and the gunner duties are bound to a named mount; anyone aboard without a duty is a Passenger (Core p.164). Warned rather than blocked — a half-filled roster is as common as a mistake.
  • Reactions are a list beside the strip rather than a fourth step, each carrying its own printed cap: Point Defence once per round, Electronic Warfare once per salvo (Core p.171, p.173).
  • Two or more weapons of the same type in one mount fire as one attack at +1 per damage die, and missiles are excluded from both that bonus and the mount multiple (Core p.168; High Guard p.29).
  • Criticals: severity is Effect − 5, a repeat takes the higher of the new severity and the old one plus one, the cap is 6, and the location table is transcribed unchanged (Core p.169).
  • A salvo is a contact of its own — everything one ship fires at one target in one round — and it crosses on the Missile Flight table read from the band it was launched at, not the band the two ships are at when it arrives (Core p.172).
  • Point Defence and Electronic Warfare are aimed at that contact and thin it: a Difficult (10+) Electronics (sensors) check takes its Effect in missiles, once per salvo per round however many operators try (Core p.173).
  • Missiles lose Smart inside Close range, a salvo launched at Distant takes the printed penalty for the crossing, and the contact carries the round at which it runs out of fuel (Core p.172).
  • On arrival the salvo attacks at DM+1 per missile still flying, with neither the gunner's skill nor the range applying, and on a hit one missile's damage is rolled and multiplied by the Effect, capped at the missiles left (Core p.173).
  • With the Companion's defence missiles switched on, a salvo carries its class — standard, dogfight, interceptor or torpedo — stored on the salvo rather than read off the rack: each class is refused a launch past its own maximum band and gains its printed DM inside it (Companion p.167).
  • With the staged defence switched on, the Point defence button gains the chapter's three layers: area defence kills one missile per hit and a torpedo on 4+, point defence a missile on 3+ and a torpedo on 5+, and close-in defence stays the reaction's own Effect (Companion p.168).
  • A container-launcher is a fitting that spends a hardpoint, which is what a hardpoint and never a firmpoint comes to on a hull whose hardpoint budget is nil (Companion p.168).

What it leaves to you

  • Close escorts are yours to run. With the Companion's chapter on saturation attacks in play, an escort is capped at a tenth of the tonnage it protects, takes 1D rounds to resume station, and may engage only threats aimed at its charge — and its gunners fire at DM+1 per additional weapon in the turret and DM−2 at a threat aimed at another vessel. None of those four reaches a die here, because this screen subtracts a typed Effect rather than rolling a point-defence attack, and no mount holds a threat of its own. What is built is the escorts' guns killing a torpedo on the same 4+ as anyone else's (Companion p.168).
  • Two design-time clauses of the defence missiles are yours. Two dogfight missiles or one interceptor per firmpoint on a rail, and four dogfight missiles or two interceptors taking the space one standard missile takes in a magazine, are both figures you apply when you build the ship: no mount here holds rails, and a magazine is stored as an absolute count rather than as a ratio (Companion p.167).

What this screen handles for you

  • The attack path does not roll to hit: "only spinal mount weapons require a roll to hit. All other attacks are assumed to hit with varying degrees of success" (High Guard p.118), so an Attack Factor is read against the Attack Effectiveness table and only a spinal mount makes a to-hit roll at all.
  • Fleet figures are ordinary space combat with the dice divided out: damage is the number of dice the ordinary weapon rolls, and Armour and Hull Points are the printed ones over 3.5, which is the average of 1D.
  • The four critical immunities by tonnage are applied as what still lands on a hull that size (High Guard p.119), and an offensively superior ship scores its extra critical.
  • The critical location is the same 2D table ordinary space combat uses, and a critical's severity is 1, the ladder being Sustained Damage counted over a different pool (High Guard p.121, p.119).
  • The five pools a round refills — salvo, meson, damper, sand and repair — are cleared and filled together (High Guard p.113, 119, 121).
  • Formation is a fleet's own spread: Adjacent-to-Close gives every ship Defensive DM+1, Short is the plane of battle, and a fleet that strays to Medium has one turn's grace to return (High Guard p.115, 117).
  • The flag ship gives its fleet DM+1 while it remains in the battle, and a hull with no command bridge is refused the role rather than warned about it (High Guard p.105, 115).
  • A fleet's Thrust is the slowest ship of the battle line, with the reserve and the squadrons out of it (High Guard p.115, 117) — a ruling this system had to make, because the book uses "the fleet's Thrust score" once and never defines it. There is a box on the screen for a referee who rules otherwise.
  • The range DM column is ordinary space combat's, with the one exception the chapter prints: no row at Distant, where the Core carries −6 (Core p.167).
  • A squadron is one ship and a count of how many are flying it, and a fighter's Armour 2 becomes squadron Armour 1 (High Guard p.114).
  • The Morale check is rolled each round off the battle rather than typed, with its four printed events and the flag ship's DM+1 as five named rows — each drawn even when it is worth nothing (High Guard p.115, 122). The book prints DMs and neither a target nor a consequence, saying only that the check "potentially result[s] in changes to the Crew Skill score", so the dice are rolled, the card is posted and the referee states what it cost.
  • Dispersal is the chapter's own task chain — Average (8+) Leadership, then Difficult (10+) Tactics (naval) — with the Fleet Dispersal table read off its Effect, the rounds and DM it charges both of a ship's DMs, and page 122's "other actions cannot be taken by ships participating in a dispersal" (High Guard p.122).
  • Breaking off costs the fleet Defensive DM−1 and locks its spinal mounts, and a fleet holding a planet as an obstruction gains Defensive DM+1 per point of Thrust superiority (High Guard p.122, 124).
  • A missile salvo is a contact with a position, a target and an age and no hull at all: launched by a ship or a wing, flown on page 119's Missile Flight table, thinned by Salvo Defence at one missile per point, and resolved on the warheads that survive (High Guard p.113, 119, 124).
  • The printed Fleet Manoeuvre Chart is a screen of its own: each fleet holds a position on the chapter's own map and the range between any two of them is derived from those positions rather than typed pair by pair (High Guard p.123).
  • The three things the chapter keeps off the Fleet Combat Weapons table stay off it — an ion weapon and a missile launcher are read at fleet scale rather than fired as direct-fire batteries, and the row says why in place of the button (High Guard p.111).

What it leaves to you

  • A Hull critical in a fleet battle is printed and not applied. High Guard takes a percentage of Adjusted Hull Points where ordinary space combat takes a flat number; the card computes the percentage, names the pool it comes out of, and leaves it to you, because the chapter gives no rule for the further criticals that damage would set off (High Guard p.120).

What this screen handles for you

  • A Study Period is eight weeks, they need not be consecutive, and each week must be fully dedicated (Core p.55) — which is why a period is drawn as eight boxes and not as a bar.
  • Improving to the next level takes as many periods as the level being reached (Core p.55).
  • The period ends on an Average (8+) check against the programme's own characteristic — EDU, except that Athletics does not use EDU and takes the physical characteristic its speciality names (Core p.55).
  • Past 3 × (INT + EDU) skill levels, a further skill can only be learned at level 0 (Core p.55). This is the same printed procedure character creation follows when its own cap is passed.
  • The Companion's engine shares the programme: a domaine d'apprentissage is a programme, and dedicated points are allocated to one and cannot be moved (Companion p.39-40).
  • Its price tables are transcribed as printed: a skill level costs its own level and doubles past the sixth; a physical characteristic costs its new value and a mental one twice that (Companion p.40).
  • SOC cannot be trained, and neither can PSI (Companion p.40) — the page names five characteristics, and psionic strength has training rules of its own.
  • A teacher is another character: reaching level N needs a teacher at N+1, and the student rolls an Average (8+) INT check at DM−N (Companion p.41-42). The teacher's level is read at the roll and never copied onto the programme, because a number copied off another sheet is stale the moment that sheet changes.
  • General Experience has no pool, deliberately: a General point is awarded and spent in the same act (Companion p.39).

What it leaves to you

  • Whether a study week was truly free is your call. A week must be fully dedicated and an interrupted one is wasted, and nothing here knows which week of campaign time a tick belongs to. The window prints the weeks logged across every open programme, which is the number to compare against the time the campaign has actually spent (Core p.55).

What this screen handles for you

  • High gravity is DM−1 until acclimatised, over 1D weeks (Core p.80), so the effect is standing: it is applied on entry and deliberately not removed when the token leaves.
  • Radiation is a one-shot dose on entry; temperature and vacuum are per-round rows on the round start.
  • Hazard damage goes onto the chain raw, from END, because Protection is what an attack meets and a hot plain is not attacking anyone (Core p.82).
  • Two books print two vacuum systems and a world setting says which is in force: the Core's escalating die per round by default, or the Companion's flat table keyed on the suit — no protection, a major breach or a minor one — against hard and partial vacuum (Core p.82, Companion p.67).

What it leaves to you

  • Every hazard interval but the combat round is yours to apply. A region states its band, its damage and how often it bites; only the per-round interval fires by itself, and only because a combat is advanced by hand. Per-minute, per-90-second and per-hour hazards are printed on the region and applied when you say so.
  • Under the Companion's vacuum table, a minimal atmosphere is yours to run. Its two columns of hard and partial vacuum bite every round and are applied for you; the third column is a point of damage per minute, per 90 seconds or per 120 seconds depending on the suit, and after a delay measured in the Traveller's own END — so the region posts the rule once when the exposure begins, and the clock is yours (Companion p.67).

What this screen handles for you

  • One demand, several Travellers: the skill or the characteristic, the difficulty, the timeframe and the stance are set once, and each roster row previews what that Traveller would bring to it before anything is sent (Core p.59, p.61).
  • How the demand names a skill is a three-state — a named skill, no skill at all, or the player's own pick — because the book makes the pairing of skill and characteristic the referee's choice "depending on the situation" (Core p.59).
  • A line may disagree with the demand it is part of: its own skill, difficulty, characteristic set or opposed partner, with unset meaning the demand decides (Core p.59, p.61).
  • A blank difficulty is a real answer and not a missing one: the book allows a check with none stated, and the card scores it against the assumed Average (8+) (Core p.61).
  • A Boon or a Bane rides the demand, one or the other and never both, and reaches the player's prompt already set (Core p.61).
  • Two lines of the same demand can be set against each other as an opposed check, the higher Effect taking it and a draw being the standstill the book describes (Core p.62).
  • A whole side can be collapsed into one roll made on the highest score in it, which is what the book asks for when two forces oppose each other (Core p.73).
  • The ambush is one rule with two signs and the sign is each line's own: DM+6 to the side that is aware, DM−6 to the side that is not, and only for the first round (Core p.73).
  • Concluding is the referee's, and it freezes one of three readings: how many answered, the rung a task chain reached, or the total Effect of every answer — which is the reading a book asks for where four checks are added together (Core p.63, Mercenary Book 1 p.47).
  • A psionic demand is rolled on the power itself with the PSI DM, and a Traveller with no points is told they cannot attempt it rather than being asked to (Core p.229).
  • A demand can be written into a journal, an adventure or an item description and opens this window already filled in, so a published scene carries its own checks.

What this screen handles for you

  • REP is an optional characteristic like the other six, off by default, on the same DM ladder, and a Traveller at REP 0 reads DM−3 like anyone at 0 (Bounty Hunter p.8).
  • A contract has two portions and one of them is given to the Travellers: the handover is a real event here, and it is what makes the two printed rolls available to the hunter at all (Bounty Hunter p.18).
  • Negotiating the bounty is 2D plus the hunter's REP DM read against the printed table — once, and it can settle the fee lower than the offer, from 40 % down to 50 % up (Bounty Hunter p.10).
  • A hunter under the client's minimum REP may ask anyway, at the difficulty the difference dictates, and a failure costs REP−1 — floored at zero, the book putting no negative REP on the sheet (Bounty Hunter p.10).
  • That difficulty is frozen with the outcome, because the failure's own REP−1 would otherwise widen the difference it was read from and the roll would no longer be reproducible.
  • A Reputation Change is 2D at DM−1 for every four REP the hunter already carries, so a name already made is the harder one to grow (Bounty Hunter p.9).
  • Only one circumstance modifies that roll — the highest applicable, never the sum — because the printed rows overlap on purpose (Bounty Hunter p.9).
  • The eight-step contract generator rolls the book's own tables in the printed order, each step writing one field, with the priority carried from the first draw into the three that depend on it (Bounty Hunter p.21-27). It needs the tables installed; without them it refuses rather than inventing a contract.

What it leaves to you

  • When a Reputation Change is rolled, and on which circumstance, is yours. The book hands you both — the roll comes "any time they do something that could have an effect on their REP", and the circumstances it prints are a list it calls non-exhaustive — so the control sits on your side of the contract and the card still speaks under the hunter's name (Bounty Hunter p.9).
